claim: Drosophila melanogaster larvae display extensive natural variation in nociceptive escape behaviors.
source: In this study, we revealed that D. melanogaster larvae display an extensive natural variation in nociceptive escape behaviors.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from 38 DGRP lines showing variation in rolling latency and probability (Figure 1C, D), and the authors explicitly state this finding in the Discussion.

claim: The strain-specific median rolling latency ranged from 2.83 s to 10 s among 38 representative DGRP strains.
source: We quantified the rolling behavior in 38 representative inbred wild-type strains of DGRP and observed a considerable variation in the behavior: the strain-specific median rolling latency ranged from 2.83 s to 10 s and the occurrence rates of rolling behavior (rolling probability) within 10 s ranged from around 30% to almost 100% among these strains (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from behavioral assays across 38 DGRP strains, with specific numerical ranges stated and supported by Figure 1C and D.

claim: The rolling probability within 10 s ranged from around 30% to almost 100% among 38 representative DGRP strains.
source: We quantified the rolling behavior in 38 representative inbred wild-type strains of DGRP and observed a considerable variation in the behavior: the strain-specific median rolling latency ranged from 2.83 s to 10 s and the occurrence rates of rolling behavior (rolling probability) within 10 s ranged from around 30% to almost 100% among these strains (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from behavioral assays across 38 DGRP strains, with specific numerical ranges stated and supported by Figure 1C and D.

claim: GWA analysis identified 37 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), two deletions, and three insertions in or near 36 candidate genes associated with nociceptive behavior.
source: We then identified in total 37 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), two deletions, and three insertions in or near 36 candidate genes (Figure 1—source data 2), at a threshold p-value of 1.0 × 10–5, a commonly used threshold p-value in previous studies with DGRP (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Mackay and Huang, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific numbers of genetic variants identified through GWA analysis using DGRP 2.0 tool, with reference to source data and figures.

claim: Pan-neuronal knockdown of CG9336 resulted in significant enhancement of rolling probability.
source: By evaluating 17 RNAi strains that were currently available, we found that pan-neuronal knockdown of the CG9336 gene resulted in significant enhancement of the rolling probability (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript describes a functional screen of RNAi strains and reports the behavioral phenotype with reference to Figure 2A showing the data.

claim: CG9336 encodes a member of the Ly6/α-neurotoxin protein superfamily.
source: bero encodes a member of the Ly6/α-neurotoxin protein superfamily, which is characterized by a three-finger structure, including various membrane-tethered and secreted polypeptides (Loughner et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript states the protein family classification with a citation to Loughner et al., 2016.

claim: Bero has a signal peptide sequence at the amino terminus.
source: Using several bioinformatics tools, we predicted a signal peptide sequence at the amino terminus, two possible glycosylation sites, a GPI-anchorage site, a putative transmembrane region at the carboxyl terminus, and five putative disulfide bridges, which are typical structural features of the Ly6/α-neurotoxin protein superfamily (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Almagro Armenteros et al., 2019; Baek et al., 2021; Eisenhaber et al., 1999; Gupta and Brunak, 2001; Krogh et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript reports bioinformatics predictions using multiple tools (SignalP-5.0, NetNGlyc-1.0, Big-PI Predictor, TMHMM-2.0) with citations to the methods.

claim: Bero has two possible glycosylation sites.
source: Using several bioinformatics tools, we predicted a signal peptide sequence at the amino terminus, two possible glycosylation sites, a GPI-anchorage site, a putative transmembrane region at the carboxyl terminus, and five putative disulfide bridges, which are typical structural features of the Ly6/α-neurotoxin protein superfamily (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Almagro Armenteros et al., 2019; Baek et al., 2021; Eisenhaber et al., 1999; Gupta and Brunak, 2001; Krogh et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript reports bioinformatics predictions using NetNGlyc-1.0 with citation to Gupta and Brunak, 2001.

claim: Bero has a GPI-anchorage site.
source: Using several bioinformatics tools, we predicted a signal peptide sequence at the amino terminus, two possible glycosylation sites, a GPI-anchorage site, a putative transmembrane region at the carboxyl terminus, and five putative disulfide bridges, which are typical structural features of the Ly6/α-neurotoxin protein superfamily (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Almagro Armenteros et al., 2019; Baek et al., 2021; Eisenhaber et al., 1999; Gupta and Brunak, 2001; Krogh et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript reports bioinformatics predictions using Big-PI Predictor with citation to Eisenhaber et al., 1999.

claim: Bero has a putative transmembrane region at the carboxyl terminus.
source: Using several bioinformatics tools, we predicted a signal peptide sequence at the amino terminus, two possible glycosylation sites, a GPI-anchorage site, a putative transmembrane region at the carboxyl terminus, and five putative disulfide bridges, which are typical structural features of the Ly6/α-neurotoxin protein superfamily (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Almagro Armenteros et al., 2019; Baek et al., 2021; Eisenhaber et al., 1999; Gupta and Brunak, 2001; Krogh et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript reports bioinformatics predictions using TMHMM-2.0 with citation to Krogh et al., 2001.

claim: Bero has five putative disulfide bridges.
source: Using several bioinformatics tools, we predicted a signal peptide sequence at the amino terminus, two possible glycosylation sites, a GPI-anchorage site, a putative transmembrane region at the carboxyl terminus, and five putative disulfide bridges, which are typical structural features of the Ly6/α-neurotoxin protein superfamily (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Almagro Armenteros et al., 2019; Baek et al., 2021; Eisenhaber et al., 1999; Gupta and Brunak, 2001; Krogh et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript reports bioinformatics predictions using AlphaFold2 with citation to Baek et al., 2021.

claim: Most DGRP core lines with the bero minor allele (C) showed higher responsiveness than those with the major allele (T) upon noxious thermal stimulations.
source: We found that most of the 38 DGRP core lines with the bero minor allele (C) showed higher responsiveness than those with the major allele (T) upon noxious thermal stimulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of DGRP lines grouped by SNP allele with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Animals with the bero minor allele have lower expression levels of bero compared with those possessing the major allele.
source: Using reverse transcriptase PCR, we compared the expression levels of bero in the larval central nervous system (CNS) among four DGPR strains that showed extremely quick or slow behavioral responses. We found that animals with the minor allele have lower expression levels of bero (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports RT-PCR data comparing bero expression levels across DGRP strains with different alleles, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both bero heterozygous (beroKO/+) and homozygous (beroKO/beroKO) mutant animals displayed enhanced rolling escape behavior.
source: Furthermore, we generated a bero null mutant line using CRISPR-mediated mutagenesis, which deleted the entire protein-coding sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E; 'Materials and methods'), and observed in HPA experiments that both bero heterozygous (beroKO/+) and homozygous (beroKO/beroKO) mutant animals displayed an enhanced rolling escape behavior (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data from CRISPR-generated mutants shown in Figure 2F.

claim: bero expression in neurons negatively regulates nociceptive escape behavior.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that bero expression in neurons negatively regulates nociceptive escape behavior.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple lines of evidence (knockdown, mutant, and overexpression experiments) to support this conclusion.

claim: Bero is expressed in insulin-producing cells (IPCs) in the larval brain.
source: We observed bero-YFP expression in several groups of peptidergic neurons specified by the bHLH transcription factor dimmed (dimm), including insulin-producing cells (IPCs) and a subset of Eclosion hormone-producing neurons (EH neurons) in the larval brain, and abdominal leucokinin-producing neurons (ABLK neurons) in the lateral region of abdominal ganglions in the larval ventral nerve cord (VNC; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression pattern analysis using bero-YFP protein trap strain with immunohistochemistry, shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Bero is expressed in a subset of Eclosion hormone-producing neurons (EH neurons) in the larval brain.
source: We observed bero-YFP expression in several groups of peptidergic neurons specified by the bHLH transcription factor dimmed (dimm), including insulin-producing cells (IPCs) and a subset of Eclosion hormone-producing neurons (EH neurons) in the larval brain, and abdominal leucokinin-producing neurons (ABLK neurons) in the lateral region of abdominal ganglions in the larval ventral nerve cord (VNC; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression pattern analysis using bero-YFP protein trap strain with immunohistochemistry, shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Bero is expressed in abdominal leucokinin-producing neurons (ABLK neurons) in the lateral region of abdominal ganglions in the larval ventral nerve cord.
source: We observed bero-YFP expression in several groups of peptidergic neurons specified by the bHLH transcription factor dimmed (dimm), including insulin-producing cells (IPCs) and a subset of Eclosion hormone-producing neurons (EH neurons) in the larval brain, and abdominal leucokinin-producing neurons (ABLK neurons) in the lateral region of abdominal ganglions in the larval ventral nerve cord (VNC; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression pattern analysis using bero-YFP protein trap strain with immunohistochemistry, shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Bero is expressed in midline glia.
source: Bero is also expressed in certain non-neuronal tissues, such as midline glia (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression pattern analysis using bero-YFP protein trap strain shown in Figure 3A.

claim: bero is expressed in all seven pairs of ABLK neurons.
source: bero is expressed in all seven pairs of ABLK neurons and is delivered to their neurites, but not expressed in any other LK neurons (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports detailed expression analysis with immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Bero is delivered to neurites of ABLK neurons.
source: bero is expressed in all seven pairs of ABLK neurons and is delivered to their neurites, but not expressed in any other LK neurons (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports detailed expression analysis with immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Bero is not expressed in any LK neurons other than ABLK neurons.
source: bero is expressed in all seven pairs of ABLK neurons and is delivered to their neurites, but not expressed in any other LK neurons (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports detailed expression analysis with immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Bero localizes on both the plasma membrane and internal membrane of ABLK neurons.
source: High-resolution imaging of individual optical sections showed that Bero localizes on both the plasma membrane and internal membrane of ABLK neurons (Figure 3C, middle).
evidence: The manuscript reports high-resolution confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bero distributes along both dendritic and axonal regions of ABLK neurons.
source: We expressed the dendrite and axon terminal markers, namely DenMark and synaptotagmin-eGFP (syt:eGFP), in ABLK neurons (Figure 3D), demonstrating that Bero distributes along both dendric and axonal regions of the neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports co-localization experiments using subcellular markers shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of bero using Lk-GAL4 caused enhanced rolling escape behavior.
source: We found that knockdown of bero using Lk-GAL4, a leucokinin-producing neuron-specific driver, caused enhanced rolling escape behavior (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell-type-specific RNAi knockdown behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Knockdown of bero using Eh-GAL4 did not result in any changes in rolling escape behavior.
source: In contrast, knockdown of bero using either Eh-GAL4, a EH neuron-specific driver, or Ilp2-GAL4, an IPC-specific driver, did not result in any changes in rolling escape behavior (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell-type-specific RNAi knockdown behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Knockdown of bero using Ilp2-GAL4 did not result in any changes in rolling escape behavior.
source: In contrast, knockdown of bero using either Eh-GAL4, a EH neuron-specific driver, or Ilp2-GAL4, an IPC-specific driver, did not result in any changes in rolling escape behavior (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript reports cell-type-specific RNAi knockdown behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: bero overexpression in ABLK neurons suppressed rolling behavior.
source: We observed that bero overexpression suppressed rolling behavior (Figure 3F), indicating that bero expression in ABLK neurons plays an essential role in the negative regulation of nociceptive behavior.
evidence: The manuscript reports ABLK-specific overexpression behavioral data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: bero expression in ABLK neurons plays an essential role in the negative regulation of nociceptive behavior.
source: We observed that bero overexpression suppressed rolling behavior (Figure 3F), indicating that bero expression in ABLK neurons plays an essential role in the negative regulation of nociceptive behavior.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the overexpression experiment results.

claim: ABLK neurons display persistent fluctuations of intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: We monitored calcium responses in ABLK neurons in fillet preparations and observed that cell bodies and neurite regions of ABLK neurons displayed persistent fluctuations of intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which was consistent with a previous study (Okusawa et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B, with citation to a previous study.

claim: Optogenetic activation of nociceptors evoked weak but reliable evoked neuronal activities in ABLK neurons.
source: Notably, optogenetic activation of the nociceptors evoked weak but reliable evoked neuronal activities in ABLK neurons, suggesting that these neurons respond to nociceptive inputs (Figure 4C and D; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports optogenetic stimulation and calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C and D, with citation to Hu et al., 2020.

claim: ABLK neurons respond to nociceptive inputs.
source: Notably, optogenetic activation of the nociceptors evoked weak but reliable evoked neuronal activities in ABLK neurons, suggesting that these neurons respond to nociceptive inputs (Figure 4C and D; Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: bero knockdown almost completely abolished persistent fluctuating activities in ABLK neurons.
source: We found that bero knockdown almost completely abolished persistent fluctuating activities (Figure 4A and B), whereas it increased the amplitude of evoked nociceptive responses (Figure 4C, D and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data comparing control and bero knockdown shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: bero knockdown increased the amplitude of evoked nociceptive responses in ABLK neurons.
source: We found that bero knockdown almost completely abolished persistent fluctuating activities (Figure 4A and B), whereas it increased the amplitude of evoked nociceptive responses (Figure 4C, D and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports calcium imaging data comparing control and bero knockdown shown in Figure 4C, D and F.

claim: bero knockdown did not affect larval free locomotion.
source: Given the phenotype of the bero knockdown on spontaneous persistent activities in ABLK neurons, we performed a behavioral analysis of undisturbed free locomotion and found that bero knockdown did not affect larval free locomotion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports locomotion analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: bero plays a critical role in generating a relatively higher level of persistent fluctuating activities in ABLK neurons.
source: Collectively, we have revealed that bero plays a critical role in not only generating a relatively higher level of persistent fluctuating activities, but also inhibiting the evoked nociceptive responses of the ABLK neurons, thereby suppressing the nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes calcium imaging data to draw this conclusion.

claim: bero plays a critical role in inhibiting the evoked nociceptive responses of ABLK neurons.
source: Collectively, we have revealed that bero plays a critical role in not only generating a relatively higher level of persistent fluctuating activities, but also inhibiting the evoked nociceptive responses of the ABLK neurons, thereby suppressing the nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes calcium imaging data to draw this conclusion.

claim: bero suppresses nociceptive escape behavior by regulating neuronal activities in ABLK neurons.
source: Collectively, we have revealed that bero plays a critical role in not only generating a relatively higher level of persistent fluctuating activities, but also inhibiting the evoked nociceptive responses of the ABLK neurons, thereby suppressing the nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes behavioral and calcium imaging data to draw this conclusion.

claim: Red light illumination of pan-LK neurons elicited robust rolling behavior that was never observed in control larvae.
source: We first activated pan-LK neurons and found that red light illumination elicited a robust rolling behavior that was never observed in control larvae (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports optogenetic activation behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of ABLK neurons almost exclusively resulted in bending behavior rather than rolling.
source: Surprisingly, optogenetic activation of ABLK neurons almost exclusively resulted in not rolling but bending behavior, which is considered as a separable initial phase of the entire sequence of escape motions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports optogenetic activation behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Activation of SELK neurons induced robust rolling behavior in all tested larvae.
source: In contrast, activation of SELK neurons induced robust rolling behavior in all tested larvae.
evidence: The manuscript reports optogenetic activation behavioral data.

claim: Silencing ABLK neurons by expressing Kir2.1 mildly enhanced rolling escape behavior.
source: To test this, we silenced ABLK neurons by expressing the inward rectifying potassium channel Kir2.1, which mildly enhanced rolling escape behavior (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports genetic silencing behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Inhibition of ABLK neurons using GtACR1 significantly impaired rolling escape behavior.
source: Inhibition of ABLK neurons using Guillardia theta anion channelrhodopsin-1 (GtACR1; Mohammad et al., 2017) significantly impaired rolling escape behavior (Figure 5E), suggesting that acute evoked activity of ABLK neurons is essential for nociceptive escape behavior.
evidence: The manuscript reports optogenetic inhibition behavioral data shown in Figure 5E, with citation to Mohammad et al., 2017.

claim: Acute evoked activity of ABLK neurons is essential for nociceptive escape behavior.
source: Inhibition of ABLK neurons using Guillardia theta anion channelrhodopsin-1 (GtACR1; Mohammad et al., 2017) significantly impaired rolling escape behavior (Figure 5E), suggesting that acute evoked activity of ABLK neurons is essential for nociceptive escape behavior.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the optogenetic inhibition experiment results.

claim: Concurrent activation of ABLK neurons resulted in significantly decreased rolling escape behavior.
source: Unexpectedly, however, concurrent activation of ABLK neurons also resulted in significantly decreased rolling escape behavior (Figure 5F).
evidence: The manuscript reports optogenetic activation combined with heat stimulation behavioral data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Proper dynamics of acute activity in ABLK neurons is essential for the facilitation of rolling escape behavior.
source: These seemingly inconsistent results suggest that the neuronal activity induced by optogenetic activation is not comparable with the naturally evoked nociceptive responses in ABLK neurons, and proper dynamics of acute activity in ABLK neurons is essential for the facilitation of the rolling escape behavior.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the combined optogenetic activation and inhibition results.

claim: ABLK neurons produce leucokinin (LK).
source: Previous studies have reported that ABLK neurons produce leucokinin (LK; de Haro et al., 2010) and corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF)-like diuretic hormone (diuretic hormone 44, DH44; Zandawala et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (de Haro et al., 2010) reporting this finding.

claim: ABLK neurons produce corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF)-like diuretic hormone (diuretic hormone 44, DH44).
source: Previous studies have reported that ABLK neurons produce leucokinin (LK; de Haro et al., 2010) and corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF)-like diuretic hormone (diuretic hormone 44, DH44; Zandawala et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies (Zandawala et al., 2018) reporting this finding.

claim: ABLK neurons express tyrosine decarboxylase 2 (Tdc2).
source: Our immunohistochemistry tests additionally identified that ABLK neurons express tyrosine decarboxylase 2 (Tdc2), a key synthetic enzyme for tyramine (TA) and octopamine (OA; Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ABLK neurons are not GABAergic.
source: In contrast, ABLK neurons are neither GABAergic, glutamatergic, nor cholinergic (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ABLK neurons are not glutamatergic.
source: In contrast, ABLK neurons are neither GABAergic, glutamatergic, nor cholinergic (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ABLK neurons are not cholinergic.
source: In contrast, ABLK neurons are neither GABAergic, glutamatergic, nor cholinergic (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Suppression of Tbh in ABLK neurons reduced rolling probability.
source: We found that suppression of Dh44 or Tbh reduced the rolling probability, indicating functional roles of DH44 and octopamine in the facilitation of nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports ABLK-specific RNAi knockdown behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Suppression of Dh44 in ABLK neurons reduced rolling probability.
source: We found that suppression of Dh44 or Tbh reduced the rolling probability, indicating functional roles of DH44 and octopamine in the facilitation of nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports ABLK-specific RNAi knockdown behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DH44 has a functional role in the facilitation of nociceptive escape behavior.
source: We found that suppression of Dh44 or Tbh reduced the rolling probability, indicating functional roles of DH44 and octopamine in the facilitation of nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the RNAi knockdown experiment results.

claim: Octopamine has a functional role in the facilitation of nociceptive escape behavior.
source: We found that suppression of Dh44 or Tbh reduced the rolling probability, indicating functional roles of DH44 and octopamine in the facilitation of nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the RNAi knockdown experiment results.

claim: The behavioral variations in a Drosophila population may provide adaptive advantages in ever-changing environments.
source: The behavioral variations in a Drosophila population may provide it with adaptive advantages in ever-changing environments, especially when coexisting with geographically and seasonally variable parasitoid wasp species (Bergland et al., 2014; Fleury et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the adaptive significance with citations to Bergland et al., 2014 and Fleury et al., 2004.

claim: Most homozygous bero mutant animals with the Canton-S background did not survive to adulthood.
source: Notably, most homozygous mutant animals with the Canton-S background did not survive to adulthood, suggesting that bero plays an essential role in animal development as well as nociception.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from maintaining the mutant line.

claim: bero plays an essential role in animal development.
source: Notably, most homozygous mutant animals with the Canton-S background did not survive to adulthood, suggesting that bero plays an essential role in animal development as well as nociception.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the lethality of homozygous mutants.

claim: Mammalian Ly6 proteins affect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR) to modulate neuronal excitability.
source: Notably, mammalian Ly6 proteins affect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChR) to modulate neuronal excitability (Tsetlin, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Tsetlin, 2015 for this established finding.

claim: Quiver (Qvr)/Sleepless (Sss) suppresses neuronal excitability by enhancing the expression levels and open probability of Shaker potassium channels.
source: A Drosophila Ly6-like protein, Quiver (Qvr)/Sleepless (Sss), plays dual roles in sleep regulation, not only suppressing neuronal excitability by enhancing the expression levels and open probability of Shaker potassium channels but also reducing cholinergic synaptic transmission by antagonizing nAChR (Wu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Wu et al., 2014 and Wu et al., 2010 for this established finding.

claim: Quiver (Qvr)/Sleepless (Sss) reduces cholinergic synaptic transmission by antagonizing nAChR.
source: A Drosophila Ly6-like protein, Quiver (Qvr)/Sleepless (Sss), plays dual roles in sleep regulation, not only suppressing neuronal excitability by enhancing the expression levels and open probability of Shaker potassium channels but also reducing cholinergic synaptic transmission by antagonizing nAChR (Wu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Wu et al., 2014 and Wu et al., 2010 for this established finding.

claim: ABLK neurons showed evoked neuronal responses upon UV/blue light stimulation.
source: A previous study reported that ABLK neurons showed evoked neuronal responses upon UV/blue light stimulation, and the responses were required for light-avoidance behavior (Imambocus et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Imambocus et al., 2022 for this finding.

claim: ABLK neuronal responses to UV/blue light stimulation are required for light-avoidance behavior.
source: A previous study reported that ABLK neurons showed evoked neuronal responses upon UV/blue light stimulation, and the responses were required for light-avoidance behavior (Imambocus et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Imambocus et al., 2022 for this finding.

claim: ABLK neurons receive converging inputs and affect differential outputs when animals encounter different modalities of noxious stimuli.
source: These findings imply that ABLK neurons receive converging inputs and affect differential outputs when animals encounter different modalities of noxious stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the combined findings about ABLK neuron responses to different stimuli.

claim: ABLK neurons have known functions in the regulation of water balance in adults.
source: ABLK neurons have known functions in the regulation of water balance and food intake in adults (Liu et al., 2015; Zandawala et al., 2018), suggesting that the persistent activities of the neurons may reflect stresses from desiccation and starvation.
evidence: The manuscript cites Liu et al., 2015 and Zandawala et al., 2018 for this established finding.

claim: ABLK neurons have known functions in the regulation of food intake in adults.
source: ABLK neurons have known functions in the regulation of water balance and food intake in adults (Liu et al., 2015; Zandawala et al., 2018), suggesting that the persistent activities of the neurons may reflect stresses from desiccation and starvation.

source: ABLK neurons have known functions in the regulation of water balance and food intake in adults (Liu et al., 2015; Zandawala et al., 2018), suggesting that the persistent activities of the neurons may reflect stresses from desiccation and starvation.

evidence: The manuscript cites Fadok et al., 2017 for this finding in mice.

claim: CRF release in the central amygdala increases mechanosensitivity and nocifensive reflexes in mice.
source: In mice, CRF+ neurons in the central amygdala mediate conditioned flight (jump escape behavior; Fadok et al., 2017), where CRF release in the central amygdala increases mechanosensitivity and nocifensive reflexes (Bourbia et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Bourbia et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2015 for this finding in mice.

claim: CRF mediates stress-induced thermal hyperalgesia in rats.
source: Moreover, CRF mediates stress-induced thermal hyperalgesia in rats (Itoga et al., 2016), suggesting that the role of DH44 in facilitating nociceptive response might be evolutionarily conserved between insects and mammals.
evidence: The manuscript cites Itoga et al., 2016 for this finding in rats.

claim: The role of DH44 in facilitating nociceptive response might be evolutionarily conserved between insects and mammals.
source: Moreover, CRF mediates stress-induced thermal hyperalgesia in rats (Itoga et al., 2016), suggesting that the role of DH44 in facilitating nociceptive response might be evolutionarily conserved between insects and mammals.

claim: bero has an essential role in monitoring stresses, which may modulate the nociceptive escape behavior.
source: Our findings thus raise the possibility that bero has an essential role in monitoring stresses, which may modulate the nociceptive escape behavior (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the broader functional role of bero based on the combined findings.

source: Our findings reveal that Bero modulates an escape response by regulating distinct neuronal activities in ABLK neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

source: Belly roll, a GPI-anchored Ly6 protein, regulates Drosophila melanogaster escape behaviors by modulating the excitability of nociceptive peptidergic interneurons
evidence: This is stated in the title and supported by bioinformatics predictions in the Results.

claim: bero knockdown in ABLK neurons resulted in enhanced escape behavior.
source: We show that Bero is expressed in abdominal leucokinin-producing neurons (ABLK neurons) and bero knockdown in ABLK neurons resulted in enhanced escape behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and supported by behavioral data in the Results.

claim: ABLK neurons responded to activation of nociceptors.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that ABLK neurons responded to activation of nociceptors and initiated the behavior.

source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that ABLK neurons responded to activation of nociceptors and initiated the behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and supported by optogenetic activation data in the Results.

claim: bero knockdown reduced persistent neuronal activity in ABLK neurons.
source: Notably, bero knockdown reduced persistent neuronal activity and increased evoked nociceptive responses in ABLK neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and supported by calcium imaging data in the Results.

claim: bero knockdown increased evoked nociceptive responses in ABLK neurons.
source: Notably, bero knockdown reduced persistent neuronal activity and increased evoked nociceptive responses in ABLK neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract and supported by calcium imaging data in the Results.

claim: When Drosophila melanogaster larvae encounter noxious stimuli, they show stereotypic escape behaviors composed of an initial abrupt bending and subsequent corkscrew-like rolling.
source: When Drosophila melanogaster larvae encounter noxious stimuli, such as harsh mechanical stimulations intrinsic to attacks by parasitoid wasps, they show stereotypic escape behaviors composed of an initial abrupt bending and subsequent corkscrew-like rolling (Hwang et al., 2007; Onodera et al., 2017; Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hwang et al., 2007; Onodera et al., 2017; Tracey et al., 2003 for this established finding.

claim: Class IV dendritic arborization neurons (Class IV neurons) sense noxious stimuli in larvae.
source: In larvae, the noxious stimuli are mainly sensed by class IV dendritic arborization neurons (Class IV neurons) underneath the body wall (Tracey et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites Tracey et al., 2003 for this established finding.

claim: v'td2 neurons detect noxious light stimuli.
source: In addition, a type of tracheal dendrite neuron (v'td2 neurons) and class III dendritic arborization neurons (Class III neurons) are known to detect noxious light stimuli and noxious cold stimuli, respectively (Imambocus et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Imambocus et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2016 for this established finding.

claim: Class III dendritic arborization neurons (Class III neurons) detect noxious cold stimuli.
source: In addition, a type of tracheal dendrite neuron (v'td2 neurons) and class III dendritic arborization neurons (Class III neurons) are known to detect noxious light stimuli and noxious cold stimuli, respectively (Imambocus et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Imambocus et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2016 for this established finding.

claim: ABLK neurons may integrate external and internal sensory stimuli, thereby orchestrating nociceptive escape behaviors.
source: Based on our results regarding the ABLK neurons, we propose that these neurons may integrate external and internal sensory stimuli, thereby orchestrating nociceptive escape behaviors.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this model based on the combined findings about ABLK neuron function.

claim: There is a large difference in the latency of rolling behavior (rolling latency) between w1118 and Canton-S strains.
source: Using the Heat Probe Assay (HPA; Tracey et al., 2003), we noticed that there is a large difference in the latency of rolling behavior (rolling latency) between the two commonly used strains, w1118 and Canton-S (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data comparing two strains shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The three response classes (rolling probability in 2, 5, and 10 s) are highly correlated with one another.
source: We categorized the rolling probability into three response classes (rolling probability in 2, 5, and 10 s) based on previous studies (Onodera et al., 2017; Terada et al., 2016; Tracey et al., 2003) and found that the three response classes are highly correlated with one another (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The bero-associated SNP (2L_20859945_SNP) is located in the second intron of CG9336 isoform A.
source: The bero-associated SNP, 2L_20859945_SNP, is located in the second intron of CG9336 isoform A (FBtr0081427) and comprises two nucleotide variations in the DGRP core 40 lines: a minor allele, cytosine, and a major allele, thymine (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic location of the SNP with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The bero-associated SNP comprises two nucleotide variations: a minor allele (cytosine) and a major allele (thymine).
source: The bero-associated SNP, 2L_20859945_SNP, is located in the second intron of CG9336 isoform A (FBtr0081427) and comprises two nucleotide variations in the DGRP core 40 lines: a minor allele, cytosine, and a major allele, thymine (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the nucleotide variations with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: ABLK-neuron-specific knockdown of Rdl enhanced rolling escape behavior upon lower thermal stimulations (44°C).
source: Consistently, our result showed that ABLK-neuron-specific knockdown of Rdl enhanced rolling escape behavior upon lower thermal stimulations (temperature of the heat probe: 44°C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports ABLK-specific RNAi knockdown behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of Rdl in all LK neurons increased the probability of escape behaviors only at low intensity of nociceptor stimulation.
source: A previous study showed that knockdown of the ionotropic GABAA receptor Resistance to dieldrin (Rdl) in all LK neurons increased the probability of escape behaviors only at low intensity of nociceptor stimulation (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hu et al., 2020 for this finding.

claim: The 5-HT1B receptor regulates larval turning behavior by changing the periodic activity level of ABLK neurons.
source: Another previous study suggested that the 5-HT1B receptor regulates larval turning behavior by changing the periodic activity level of ABLK neurons (Okusawa et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Okusawa et al., 2014 for this finding.

claim: Suppression of 5-HT1B in ABLK neurons did not show any significant effects on rolling escape behavior.
source: We examined the effects of ABLK-neuron-specific knockdown of 5-HT1B on rolling escape behavior in HPA experiments and found that the suppression of 5-HT1B did not show any significant effects (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports ABLK-specific RNAi knockdown behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.
